help.title: What do these words mean?
help.colours: Green, amber and red: green means there is enough water for paddy; amber means less water, so grow a smaller or shorter crop; red means too little water for paddy.
help.yala: Yala: the smaller, drier cultivation season, roughly April to August.
help.maha: Maha: the main cultivation season, with the north-east monsoon rains, roughly October to January.
help.bethma: Bethma: in a dry season, farmers agree to cultivate only part of the fields, usually those nearest the tank, and share that land among everyone.
help.short_paddy: Short-duration paddy: rice varieties that ripen sooner, so they need water for fewer weeks.
help.ofc: Other field crops: crops such as mung bean, cowpea and black gram, which need much less water than paddy and also feed the soil.
help.elnino: El Niño: a change in the Pacific Ocean that can change Sri Lanka's rain. Some El Niño years bring dry seasons.
help.satellite: Where the numbers come from: NASA satellites measure the water in the tank, and NASA weather data shows the rain and heat in your area.

how.title: How TerraOrb works
how.subtitle: From satellites in space to a plain answer for your tank, and how far you can trust it.
how.flow.title: From space to your field
how.flow.lead: Four steps turn satellite measurements into advice you can use.
how.step.satellite.title: Satellites watch
how.step.satellite.text: NASA satellites measure rain, temperature and the water in tanks, every day.
how.step.clean.title: We check the data
how.step.clean.text: A computer program downloads it and checks it. If something looks wrong, it stops and tells us instead of guessing.
how.step.rules.title: Fixed rules decide
how.step.rules.text: Published rules turn the numbers into a colour and into how much water each crop needs. There is no AI guessing inside the app.
how.step.advice.title: You get simple advice
how.step.advice.text: A plain answer for your tank in Sinhala or English, with the source of every number.
how.data.title: Where the data comes from
how.data.lead: Most data is from NASA. Anything that is not from NASA is labelled "Not NASA".
how.status.measured: Measured so far for {n} tank(s); the rest are waiting.
how.ds.power.name: NASA POWER
how.ds.power.what: Daily rain and temperature for every part of Sri Lanka since 1981, in squares about 50 km wide.
how.ds.power.use: Rain history, when the rains start, hot and dry spells, and how much water crops need.
how.ds.opera.name: NASA OPERA DSWx-HLS and HLS
how.ds.opera.what: Satellite maps that show where there is water, so we can measure how big each tank's water is.
how.ds.opera.use: The tank water signal: this year's water compared with other years.
how.ds.gibs.name: NASA GIBS (GPM IMERG and VIIRS)
how.ds.gibs.what: Satellite pictures of rain and clouds, and the satellite map you see behind the tanks.
how.ds.gibs.use: The rain and cloud map on the Weather page, and the main map.
how.ds.cmr.name: NASA CMR
how.ds.cmr.what: NASA's catalogue. It tells us which satellite pictures cover each tank.
how.ds.cmr.use: Finding the right pictures for every tank.
how.ds.openmeteo.name: Open-Meteo
how.ds.openmeteo.what: A free weather service that combines forecasts from weather models.
how.ds.openmeteo.use: The 16-day forecast and the live weather. This is not NASA data.
how.ds.osm.name: OpenStreetMap
how.ds.osm.what: A shared world map made by volunteers.
how.ds.osm.use: The names, places and outlines of the tanks.
how.ds.fao.name: FAO and the Department of Agriculture
how.ds.fao.what: Published guides on how much water each crop needs and how long it takes to grow.
how.ds.fao.use: The crop advice and the sowing calendar.
how.proof.title: Does the advice work?
how.proof.none: The test results are not available yet.
how.proof.intro: We tested the crop advice on years it had never seen: it learned from {train} and was then checked against {test}.
how.proof.guess: Just guessing the most common answer
how.proof.good: When we said "good to sow", the rain was enough
how.proof.beats: The advice did better than guessing ({n} cases tested).
how.proof.notbeats: The advice did not do better than guessing ({n} cases tested), so it should not be trusted.
how.proof.caveat.title: Keep in mind
how.proof.caveat: Much of this success is simply knowing the wet and dry seasons. The 16-day forecast part cannot be tested, because past forecasts were not saved. Paddy is not tested here.
how.proof.elnino.title: El Niño outlook
how.proof.elnino: The El Niño outlook did not pass its test, so the app shows it only as a plain count of past years, never as a forecast.
how.proof.tank.title: Tank water prediction
how.proof.tank: A model to predict tank water was tested on only {n} demo tanks and did not beat simply using the usual level (average error {model} points against {base}). We do not use it.
how.limits.title: What to keep in mind
how.limit.crops: The crop water numbers are drafts from FAO and Department of Agriculture pages. An Agricultural Instructor has not checked them yet.
how.limit.water: Satellite tank water has been measured for only a few tanks so far. For the others the app says "Water not checked yet".
how.limit.rain_grid: Rain data comes in squares about 50 km wide, so neighbouring villages can show the same rain.
how.limit.rain_end: NASA's newest rain data was wrong for October 2026, so we skip it. Our rain history currently ends on 30 September 2026.
how.limit.forecast: The 16-day forecast is less certain after the first week.
how.limit.thresholds: The rules and thresholds have not yet been checked by the Department of Agriculture.
how.limit.sinhala: The Sinhala text is a draft and needs a native speaker to review it.
how.limit.aid: TerraOrb is a decision aid. It does not replace advice from your Agricultural Instructor.

challenge.quiz.maha.q: Which of these describes the Maha season?
challenge.quiz.maha.o1: The smaller, drier season, roughly April to August.
challenge.quiz.maha.o2: The main cultivation season with the north-east monsoon rains, roughly October to January.
challenge.quiz.maha.o3: The months with no rain at all.
challenge.quiz.maha.why: Maha is the main season. Yala is the smaller, drier one.
challenge.quiz.wewa.q: What is a village tank (wewa) mainly for?
challenge.quiz.wewa.o1: Storing rain water so fields can be watered later.
challenge.quiz.wewa.o3: Stopping the rain from reaching the fields.
challenge.quiz.wewa.why: Tanks catch and store rain so farmers can water their fields in the weeks without rain.
challenge.quiz.water_need.q: Which crop usually needs the most water over its whole life?
challenge.quiz.water_need.why: At {tank}, paddy needs about {paddy} mm of water, while mung bean needs about {mung} mm. Paddy fields are also kept flooded, which uses a lot of water.
challenge.quiz.late_rain.q: The rains are starting late this season. Which choice is safer?
challenge.quiz.late_rain.o1: A long-duration crop that needs water for many weeks.
challenge.quiz.late_rain.o2: A short-duration crop that needs water for fewer weeks.
challenge.quiz.late_rain.o3: Plant everything and hope for the best.
challenge.quiz.late_rain.why: A shorter crop needs water for fewer weeks, so it is safer when the water may run out early.
challenge.quiz.red.q: The water signal for a tank is red. What does that mean?
challenge.quiz.red.o1: There is more water than usual.
challenge.quiz.red.o3: There is far too little water for paddy this season.
challenge.quiz.red.why: Red means a severe shortage. Other field crops that need much less water are the better choice.
challenge.quiz.bethma.o1: Sharing part of the tank's fields among all farmers in a dry season.
challenge.quiz.bethma.why: Under bethma, farmers agree to cultivate only part of the land, often the part nearest the tank, and share it fairly.
challenge.quiz.legumes.q: Why do farmers like to grow mung bean, cowpea or black gram?
challenge.quiz.legumes.o1: They need more water than paddy.
challenge.quiz.legumes.o2: They need little water and also put nitrogen back into the soil.
challenge.quiz.legumes.why: These legumes have bacteria on their roots that take nitrogen from the air, which helps the next crop.
challenge.quiz.elnino.o1: A change in Pacific Ocean temperatures that can change Sri Lanka's rain.
challenge.quiz.elnino.why: In some El Niño years Sri Lanka's seasons are drier, but not in every year. It is a hint, not a promise.
challenge.quiz.evaporation.q: On a hot, dry day, where does some of the tank's water go?
challenge.quiz.evaporation.why: Sun and heat turn some water into vapour. Hot, dry weather means tanks and crops lose water faster.
challenge.quiz.not_nasa.q: Which of these does this website NOT get from NASA?
challenge.quiz.not_nasa.why: The forecast comes from Open-Meteo weather models. The website labels everything that is not NASA data.
challenge.quiz.forecast.q: How much can we trust a 16-day rain forecast?
challenge.quiz.forecast.o2: More in the first week, and less certain after that.
challenge.quiz.forecast.why: Forecasts get less certain the further ahead they look. Trust the first days more than the last.
challenge.quiz.check_signal.q: Why look at the water signal before choosing what to plant?
challenge.quiz.check_signal.o1: To match the crop to the water you really have.
challenge.quiz.check_signal.o3: To decide the price of rice.
challenge.quiz.check_signal.why: A crop that fits the water available avoids losing the harvest in the middle of the season.
challenge.quiz.irrigated.q: Which crop is usually grown with irrigation, because rain alone often is not enough?
challenge.quiz.irrigated.why: Big onion is usually irrigated. On this website, crops that are usually irrigated carry a note saying so.
challenge.quiz.clouds.q: Why can satellites sometimes not measure a tank's water?
challenge.quiz.clouds.o1: The tank is too small to exist.
challenge.quiz.clouds.o2: Tanks are always empty at night.
challenge.quiz.clouds.o3: Clouds can hide the water from the satellite.
challenge.quiz.clouds.why: Many pictures of a tank are unusable because of cloud, especially in the rainy season.

dsp.power.name: NASA POWER
dsp.power.what: Daily rain and the daily highest and lowest temperature for every place since 1981. NASA models these from satellites and weather observations (MERRA-2) in squares about 50 km wide, so neighbouring tanks can share the same values.
dsp.power.used: Rain history, when the rains start, hot and dry spells, the usual rain, how much water crops need, and the accuracy tests.
dsp.power.note: Known problem: NASA's newest near-real-time values (from 1 October 2026) were about 24 times too large, so we skip them. Our rain history currently ends on 30 September 2026.
dsp.dswx.name: NASA OPERA DSWx-HLS
dsp.dswx.provider: NASA (OPERA project), through Earthdata and PO.DAAC
dsp.dswx.what: Surface-water maps with 30 m pixels, made from Landsat and Sentinel-2 satellite pictures (product OPERA_L3_DSWX-HLS_V1). They show where there is open water.
dsp.dswx.used: The tank water signal: how big each tank's water is now compared with other years.
dsp.dswx.note: Clouds hide the water in many pictures. Measured so far for {n} of {tanks} tanks; the others show "Water not checked yet".
dsp.hls.name: NASA HLS (Landsat and Sentinel-2)
dsp.hls.what: Satellite surface-reflectance pictures (HLSL30 and HLSS30, version 2.0). A water index (NDWI) can be worked out from them.
dsp.hls.used: A backup way to measure tank water when the DSWx maps are not available.
dsp.hls.note: Backup only: not used for any tank so far.
dsp.gibs.name: NASA GIBS satellite imagery
dsp.gibs.what: Ready-made satellite pictures: MODIS true colour (the map behind the tanks), GPM IMERG rain rate, and VIIRS true colour (the cloud picture).
dsp.gibs.used: The main map, and the rain and cloud map on each tank's Weather page.
dsp.gibs.note: These are pictures only: no numbers are taken from them.

dsp.cmr.used: Finding the right DSWx and HLS pictures for every tank.

lh.card.lessons.title: Little Lessons
lh.card.lessons.text: Picture stories about rain, seasons, village tanks, satellites, sharing, crops, forecasts, growing, wildfires, landslides, El Niño, La Niña, carbon, global warming, the water cycle and glaciers, each with a small game. Sixteen lessons for children.
ls.water.title: The journey of a raindrop
ls.water.about: How water goes up, makes clouds and falls as rain.
ls.water.s1.t: The sun warms the water in the tank. Tiny drops rise up into the sky. This is called evaporation.
ls.water.s2.t: High in the sky the tiny drops gather together. Together they make a cloud.
ls.water.s3.t: When the cloud is full, rain falls. It fills the tank and waters the fields.
ls.water.learned: The sun lifts water into the sky, clouds form, and rain brings the water back to the tanks.
ls.seasons.title: Maha and Yala
ls.seasons.about: The two farming seasons of the Dry Zone.
ls.seasons.s1.t: Maha is the main rainy season, from about October to January. The rain fills the tanks, and farmers grow paddy.
ls.seasons.s2.t: Yala is the drier season, from about May to August. The tank has less water, so farmers choose crops that drink less, like mung bean.
ls.seasons.s3.h: Look at the sky and the tank
ls.seasons.s3.t: A wise farmer looks at the sky and the tank before choosing a crop. TerraOrb helps with this.
ls.seasons.i4: Mung bean grows with little water
ls.seasons.learned: Maha is the main rainy season and Yala is the drier one. Crops that drink less suit Yala.
ls.cascade.title: A chain of tanks
ls.cascade.about: How village tanks share water, one after another.
ls.cascade.s1.t: Many villages have a chain of tanks, called a cascade. Water not used in the top tank flows down to the next tank.
ls.cascade.s2.t: Farmers let the water out through a sluice gate. When they share fairly, everyone gets some water.
ls.cascade.s3.t: The long earth wall of a tank is called a bund. Big trees keep it strong, and birds and buffalo love the water too.
ls.cascade.q1: What do we call a chain of village tanks?
ls.cascade.q2: Where does extra water from the top tank go?
ls.cascade.q3: What is the earth wall of a tank called?
ls.cascade.learned: Tanks work together in a chain called a cascade, and farmers share the water fairly.
ls.sat.title: Eyes in the sky
ls.sat.about: How satellites help us see rain and water.
ls.sat.s1.t: A satellite is a machine that circles the Earth, high above us. It looks down at the land, the clouds and the water.
ls.sat.s2.t: NASA satellites help measure rain, heat and water on the ground. They keep measuring, day after day.
ls.sat.s3.t: TerraOrb turns this data into simple advice. Satellites are only a guide, so what farmers know about their village matters too.
ls.sat.i2: What a farmer wants to grow
ls.sat.i4: A fish deep in the tank
ls.sat.learned: Satellites can see clouds, heat and water from space, but they cannot know what a farmer wants or knows.
ls.bethma.title: Bethma: sharing in dry times
ls.bethma.about: How villages share land and water when the tank runs low.
ls.bethma.s1.t: In a dry year the tank does not have enough water for every field. The farmers meet under a big tree to talk about it.
ls.bethma.s2.t: Bethma is a village custom. The farmers divide the field into small plots, so a little water can reach every family.
ls.bethma.s3.t: At harvest time every family has some rice. Sharing helps the whole village get through the dry season.
ls.bethma.o2: They divide the field into plots
ls.bethma.learned: In a dry year, villages can share land and water (bethma) so every family gets a harvest.
ls.crops.title: Big drinkers, small sippers
ls.crops.about: Which crops need a lot of water and which need little.
ls.crops.s1.t: Paddy grows in standing water, so it needs a lot of water from the tank.
ls.crops.s2.t: Mung bean, cowpea, sesame and finger millet need much less water. They can still grow when the tank is low.
ls.crops.s3.t: A wise farmer picks crops to match the water in the tank. TerraOrb shows which crops fit this season.
ls.crops.i4: A plant that grows standing in water
ls.crops.learned: Paddy needs a lot of water. Crops like mung bean and finger millet need little. Choose crops to fit the tank.
ls.forecast.title: Reading the weather
ls.forecast.about: How a forecast helps farmers plan ahead.
ls.forecast.s1.t: A forecast tells us what the weather may do in the next days. TerraOrb shows a 16-day forecast for each tank. It comes from Open-Meteo, not from NASA.
ls.forecast.s2.t: When dark clouds and rain are coming, farmers can cover their harvest and keep it dry.
ls.forecast.s3.t: Seeds grow best when rain comes soon after sowing. A forecast helps to pick a good day. A forecast can be wrong, so keep watching the sky too.
ls.forecast.q1: What does a weather forecast tell us?
ls.forecast.q1.a2: What the weather may do in the coming days
ls.forecast.q2: Dark clouds and rain are coming. What can a farmer do?
ls.forecast.q2.a1: Cover the harvest and keep it dry
ls.forecast.q3: When is a good time to sow seeds?
ls.forecast.q3.a1: In the middle of a long dry spell
ls.forecast.q3.a2: Never, seeds do not need rain
ls.forecast.learned: A forecast says what weather may come. Use it to plan, but remember it can be wrong.
ls.sowing.title: From seed to harvest
ls.sowing.about: The life of a crop, step by step.
ls.sowing.s1.t: The farmer prepares the soil and sows the seeds in neat rows.
ls.sowing.s2.t: With enough water, tiny seedlings push up and grow strong.
ls.sowing.s3.t: After some weeks or months the crop is ready. Short-duration crops are ready sooner, so they need less water.
ls.sowing.learned: A crop goes from seed to seedling to harvest. Crops that finish sooner need less water.

ls.fire.title: Fire in the dry forest
ls.fire.about: How a small spark becomes a big fire, and how we stop it.
ls.fire.learned: Dry grass burns easily. Put out campfires, make fire breaks and tell the forest officer about smoke. Satellites can spot fires from space.
ls.fire.s1.t: In the dry season the grass and leaves are very dry. A fire needs three things: something to burn, heat and air. A small spark or a campfire left alone can start it.
ls.fire.s2.t: The wind pushes the flames through the dry grass. Smoke rises and the animals run to safe places. A big fire can burn trees, farms and homes.
ls.fire.s3.t: Put out every campfire with water. People clear a strip of bare earth called a fire break. NASA satellites can see fires from space, so forest officers can find them early.

ls.fire.i3: Throwing a lit match on dry grass
ls.fire.i5: Burning rubbish next to dry grass

ls.slide.title: When a hill slides
ls.slide.about: Why heavy rain can make a hillside slide, and how trees and warnings keep us safe.
ls.slide.learned: Heavy rain on a steep hill can make the soil slide. Tree roots hold the soil. Listen to warnings and move to a safe place.
ls.slide.s1.h: Heavy rain on a steep hill
ls.slide.s1.t: Very heavy rain soaks into the soil of a steep hillside. The soil drinks the water and becomes heavy and slippery.
ls.slide.s2.t: When the soil cannot hold any more water, it can slide down the slope with mud and rocks. This is called a landslide. It can happen very fast.
ls.slide.s3.t: Tree roots hold the soil like strong fingers. Planting trees and making terraces helps. When officers say a landslide may come, go to a safe place. NASA uses satellite rain data to find places where landslides may happen.
ls.slide.q1: What can make a steep hillside slide?
ls.slide.q2: What do tree roots do on a hill?

ls.elnino.title: El Niño: a warm sea
ls.elnino.about: How a warm patch of sea far away can change the rain.
ls.elnino.learned: El Niño is a warm patch of sea in the Pacific. It can change the rain around the world, including some seasons in Sri Lanka, so we watch it and get ready.
ls.elnino.s1.t: Far away in the Pacific Ocean, the sea sometimes becomes warmer than usual for many months. Scientists call this El Niño.
ls.elnino.s2.t: The warm sea changes the winds and the clouds. Some places get less rain than usual and other places get more.
ls.elnino.s3.t: El Niño does not always bring the same weather to Sri Lanka, so it is only a hint. Farmers and scientists watch the sea and the rain, save water and choose crops that need less water.
ls.carbon.title: Carbon goes round
ls.carbon.about: How carbon moves between the air, plants, animals and the soil.
ls.carbon.learned: Carbon dioxide goes round between the air, plants, animals and the soil. Extra carbon dioxide from burning warms the Earth, and trees help take it back.
ls.carbon.s1.h: Plants take carbon from the air
ls.carbon.s1.t: Plants take a gas called carbon dioxide from the air. With sunlight and water they use it to grow leaves, wood and rice.
ls.carbon.s2.t: Animals and people eat plants and breathe out carbon dioxide. Dead leaves rot in the soil and give carbon dioxide back to the air. So carbon goes round and round.
ls.carbon.s3.t: Burning fuel in vehicles and factories, and burning forests, puts extra carbon dioxide into the air. It holds heat like a blanket and warms the Earth. Planting trees helps. NASA satellites measure carbon dioxide in the air.

ls.cycle.title: The big water cycle
ls.cycle.about: How water travels from the sea to the sky, to the tank, and back.
ls.cycle.learned: Water goes round and round: the sun lifts it up, clouds form, rain falls, and rivers and tanks carry it back.
ls.cycle.s1.t: The sun warms the sea, rivers, tanks and even leaves. Water turns into a gas called water vapour and rises into the air. This is called evaporation.
ls.cycle.s2.t: High up it is cold. The vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops of water. Billions of drops make a cloud. The wind carries clouds over the land and the hills.
ls.cycle.s3.h: Water comes down and goes round
ls.cycle.s3.t: Rain falls on the hills. It runs into streams, tanks and rivers, and some soaks into the ground. Rivers carry water back to the sea, and the journey starts again.

ls.ice.title: Melting glaciers
ls.ice.about: What glaciers are, and why melting ice makes the sea rise.
ls.ice.learned: Glaciers are rivers of ice in cold places. A warmer world melts them, and the water makes the sea rise.
ls.ice.s1.t: In very cold, high mountains and near the poles, snow piles up and turns into thick ice. A glacier is a huge, slow river of ice.
ls.ice.s2.t: When the air gets warmer, glaciers melt faster. The ice turns into water that runs away in streams.
ls.ice.s3.t: The water runs to the sea and the sea level rises a little. Sri Lanka has no glaciers, but our coasts feel the rising sea. NASA satellites measure how much ice is left.

ls.lanina.title: La Niña: a cool sea
ls.lanina.about: The cool twin of El Niño, and how it can change the rain.
ls.lanina.learned: La Niña is a cool patch of sea in the Pacific. It can change the rain around the world, including in Sri Lanka, so scientists watch it and we get ready.
ls.lanina.s1.t: In the Pacific Ocean the sea along the equator sometimes becomes cooler than usual for many months. Scientists call this La Niña. It is the opposite of El Niño.
ls.lanina.s2.t: During La Niña the winds blowing across the Pacific get stronger. They push warm water and rain clouds toward Asia and Australia. Some places get more rain and floods, and other places get less rain and drought.
ls.lanina.s3.t: La Niña does not always bring the same weather to Sri Lanka, so it is only a hint. Satellites and buoys watch the sea. NASA satellites measure how warm the sea is and how high it is. Farmers and officers use the warnings to plan water.

ls.warming.title: What is global warming?
ls.warming.about: Why the Earth is getting warmer, and what it changes.
ls.warming.learned: Gases like carbon dioxide act like a blanket. Burning fuel and cutting forests make it thicker, so the Earth warms. We can adapt and also burn less.
ls.warming.s1.t: The Earth is wrapped in a thin blanket of gases, such as carbon dioxide. The blanket keeps some of the Sun's heat near the Earth. That keeps our planet warm enough for life.
ls.warming.s2.t: Burning coal, oil and gas, and cutting down forests, add extra carbon dioxide to the air. The blanket gets thicker and holds more heat. The Earth has warmed by more than 1 degree Celsius since the late 1800s. This is global warming.
ls.warming.s3.t: A warmer Earth melts ice, raises the sea, and brings more heat waves, heavier rain at times and longer dry spells. Farmers can adapt by saving water, choosing crops that need less water, and planting trees. NASA satellites and thermometers measure the warming.
